providers.name: Wisetack
providers.tagline: Pay-over-time financing embedded in home-service software, with a flat merchant fee
providers.pricing_summary: Wisetack charges the business a flat 3.9% fee per financed transaction, which includes a 0% APR option for 3 months. Optional 0% APR add-ons cost 4.9% (6 months), 6.9% (12 months) or 9.9% (24 months), charged only when a customer qualifies for and selects that option. Customer offers range 0%-35.9% APR over 3-120 months; jobs from $500 to $65,000.
providers.apr_range: 0%-35.9% APR (customer); based on amount and credit, terms 3-120 months
providers.contractor_cost: 3.9% per financed transaction; 4.9%, 6.9% or 9.9% only when a customer selects a 6, 12 or 24-month 0% APR add-on
providers.long_description:
Wisetack is a consumer-financing platform for service businesses, including HVAC, plumbing, electrical, roofing and many other home-service trades. Wisetack says it was founded in 2018 in San Francisco, and it is backed by Insight Partners, Greylock, Quadrille Capital and Bain Capital Ventures. Loans come from its lending partners: its lenders page names Hatch Bank, U.S. Bank and Happen Bank, and in April 2026 Wisetack announced that LendingClub would underwrite and originate home improvement loans through its platform.

Wisetack says it is integrated into 30+ software platforms and names Housecall Pro, Jobber, JobNimbus, FieldPulse, Contractor Plus and others. The business sends a financing link by text or on the invoice, and the customer checks options on their phone. Wisetack says checking options does not affect the customer's credit scores.

The merchant cost is published. The business pays a flat 3.9% fee on each financed job, and that rate includes a 0% APR option for 3 months. Longer 0% APR add-ons cost 4.9% for 6 months, 6.9% for 12 months and 9.9% for 24 months, and the higher fee applies only when a customer qualifies for and picks that option. Customer offers range from 0% to 35.9% APR over 3 to 120 months, and jobs from $500 to $65,000 are covered (the cap was $25,000 until June 2026). Wisetack says funds reach the business by bank transfer, usually within 1-3 business days.

The trade-off: the fee comes out of your margin on every financed job, long 0% promotions cost up to 9.9%, and customer approval and rates depend on credit. Projects above $65,000 need a different lender.
providers.how_it_works: Turn on Wisetack inside a supported field-service app or use Wisetack's own merchant portal. Send the customer a financing link by text or on the invoice. The customer checks their options, which Wisetack says does not affect their credit scores, then picks a monthly plan. Offers range 0%-35.9% APR over 3-120 months based on the amount and the customer's credit. Once the customer confirms, Wisetack says funds are sent to your bank by ACH, landing within 1-3 business days. You pay 3.9% of each financed job, or 4.9%, 6.9% or 9.9% when the customer selects a 6, 12 or 24-month 0% APR add-on you have enabled.

pros_detail.title: Built into field-service software
pros_detail.explanation: Wisetack says it is integrated into 30+ software platforms, including Housecall Pro, Jobber, JobNimbus, FieldPulse and Contractor Plus, so contractors on those platforms can offer it from the invoice they already send.

pros_detail.title: Published merchant fee
pros_detail.explanation: Wisetack publishes its fees: 3.9% per financed transaction, rising to 4.9%, 6.9% or 9.9% only when a customer picks a 6, 12 or 24-month 0% APR add-on.

pros_detail.title: No credit impact to check options
pros_detail.explanation: Wisetack says checking financing options does not affect a customer's credit scores, which lowers the barrier to asking.

pros_detail.title: Jobs from $500 to $65,000
pros_detail.explanation: Jobs from $500 to $65,000 are eligible, with terms from 3 to 120 months, so the same tool fits a repair and a system replacement.

pros_detail.title: Paid by bank transfer
pros_detail.explanation: Wisetack says funds are sent after the customer confirms and land in your account within 1-3 business days, so you are not waiting on installments.

cons_detail.title: A fee on every financed job
cons_detail.explanation: The 3.9% fee comes out of your margin, so it needs to be priced into jobs or treated as a sales cost.

cons_detail.title: Long 0% promotions cost more
cons_detail.explanation: 0% APR for 6, 12 or 24 months costs 4.9%, 6.9% or 9.9% of the job when the customer selects it.

cons_detail.title: Customer APR can be high
cons_detail.explanation: Outside 0% promotions, offers go up to 35.9% APR depending on credit.

cons_detail.title: $65,000 ceiling
cons_detail.explanation: Larger remodels and additions above $65,000 need a different lender.

cons_detail.title: Approval depends on credit
cons_detail.explanation: All financing is subject to credit approval, and Wisetack notes that not all merchants and lending partners participate in 0% programs.

providers.best_for: Home-service contractors who want pay-over-time financing sent from the field-service software they already use, with a published per-job fee, for jobs from $500 to $65,000
providers.weaknesses: 3.9% fee on every financed job; 0% APR add-ons cost 4.9%-9.9%; customer APR up to 35.9%; $65,000 maximum
providers.affiliate_payout_note: No confirmed affiliate program; we currently earn nothing from Wisetack

faqs.q: How much does Wisetack cost the contractor?
faqs.a: Wisetack charges a flat 3.9% fee per financed transaction, which includes a 0% APR option for 3 months. If you enable longer 0% APR add-ons, the fee is 4.9% for 6 months, 6.9% for 12 months and 9.9% for 24 months, charged only when a customer qualifies for and selects that option.

faqs.q: Does checking Wisetack options hurt my customer's credit?
faqs.a: Wisetack says checking financing options does not impact a customer's credit scores. All financing is subject to credit approval, and offers depend on the amount and the customer's credit.

faqs.q: How much can customers finance, and at what rates?
faqs.a: Jobs from $500 to $65,000, over 3 to 120 months, at 0% to 35.9% APR depending on the amount and credit. Wisetack raised its limit from $25,000 to $65,000 in June 2026 and says 7- and 10-year terms start at 9.9% APR for qualified borrowers.

faqs.q: When does the contractor get paid?
faqs.a: Wisetack says that once the customer confirms, funds are sent to your bank by ACH and usually arrive within 1-3 business days, depending on your bank. The customer repays the lender over time.

faqs.q: Will Wisetack work with my software?
faqs.a: Wisetack says it is integrated into 30+ software platforms, including Housecall Pro, Jobber, JobNimbus, FieldPulse and Contractor Plus. It also has its own merchant portal if your software is not on the list.

providers.name: GreenSky
providers.tagline: Bank-funded point-of-sale home-improvement loan program for contractors
providers.pricing_summary: Merchants pay GreenSky a transaction fee on each financed sale, calculated as a percentage of the loan amount and set by GreenSky (per federal court records). GreenSky's fee schedule, customer rates and loan limits could not be confirmed from its own site. Loans are funded by GreenSky's bank partners, and its programs include deferred-interest promotional loans.
providers.apr_range: Varies by plan and bank partner; not confirmed from a GreenSky disclosure
providers.loan_range: Not confirmed from GreenSky; the CFPB described its loans as a few thousand to tens of thousands of dollars
providers.contractor_cost: Transaction fee on each financed sale, a percentage of the loan amount set by GreenSky; get the rate for each plan in writing before enrolling
providers.long_description:
GreenSky runs a point-of-sale lending program that lets home-improvement contractors offer financing to homeowners. GreenSky does not fund the loans itself: bank partners do. A 2026 KBRA rating release names Synovus Bank and Comenity Capital Bank as originators of GreenSky loans and says GreenSky was founded in 2006 and is headquartered in Atlanta. GreenSky was owned by Goldman Sachs until March 15, 2024, when a consortium led by Sixth Street, with KKR, Bayview Asset Management and CardWorks, completed its purchase.

The contractor offers GreenSky financing with a quote, the customer applies, and loan proceeds are paid to the contractor rather than the customer, as the CFPB has described. The contractor pays GreenSky a transaction fee on each financed sale, calculated as a percentage of the loan amount and set by GreenSky. GreenSky's programs include deferred-interest promotional loans. Its fee schedule, customer rates and loan limits could not be confirmed from its own site.

GreenSky has a regulatory record contractors should know. In 2021 the CFPB found it had originated thousands of loans consumers did not request or authorize, and in May 2026 it settled a multistate investigation by five states and the District of Columbia into loans that businesses offering GreenSky financing took out in consumers' names without consent. A federal court in California certified a class of borrowers in 2025 in a case over GreenSky's transaction fees, and the case was still active in September 2026.

The trade-off: GreenSky gives contractors a bank-funded financing program for large home-improvement jobs, but the fee is not public, deferred-interest promotions need careful explanation, and every loan must be clearly authorized by the customer.
providers.how_it_works: You enroll as a GreenSky merchant and offer its financing plans alongside your quote. The customer applies through GreenSky's platform, and one of GreenSky's bank partners decides whether to lend. When the customer's loan is used to pay for the job, the proceeds go to you, minus GreenSky's transaction fee, which is a percentage of the loan amount set by GreenSky and varies by plan. The customer repays the loan over time. Some plans are deferred-interest promotions, so explain the promotional terms and make sure the customer personally authorizes the loan.

pros_detail.title: Bank-funded program
pros_detail.explanation: Loans are funded by GreenSky's bank partners; a 2026 KBRA release names Synovus Bank and Comenity Capital Bank as originators.

pros_detail.title: Contractor is paid from the loan
pros_detail.explanation: The CFPB describes GreenSky loan proceeds as going directly to the merchant, so you are not waiting on the customer's installments.

pros_detail.title: Promotional plans available
pros_detail.explanation: GreenSky's programs include deferred-interest promotional loans, which can help a customer fit a large project into a budget.

pros_detail.title: Large, established program
pros_detail.explanation: GreenSky said in March 2024 that it had served nearly 6 million consumers and had over 10,000 merchants in its network.

cons_detail.title: Fee not published
cons_detail.explanation: The transaction fee is a percentage of each loan set by GreenSky, and no fee schedule could be read on GreenSky's site. Get the rate for every plan in writing.

cons_detail.title: Regulatory history
cons_detail.explanation: A 2021 CFPB consent order and a May 2026 multistate settlement both involved loans taken out in consumers' names without their authorization.

cons_detail.title: Pending fee class action
cons_detail.explanation: A federal court certified a class of California borrowers in January 2025 in a case over GreenSky's transaction fees; the case was still active in September 2026.

cons_detail.title: Deferred-interest terms need explaining
cons_detail.explanation: On deferred-interest plans, interest that builds up during the promotion can be charged if the balance is not paid in full in time. Customers need to understand that before signing.

cons_detail.title: Terms not confirmable online
cons_detail.explanation: Customer rates and loan limits could not be confirmed from GreenSky's own pages, so you depend on the enrollment paperwork.

providers.best_for: Home-improvement contractors on larger projects who want a bank-funded point-of-sale loan program and are prepared to price in a transaction fee and explain promotional terms carefully
providers.weaknesses: Transaction fee is set by GreenSky and not published; 2021 CFPB consent order and 2026 multistate settlement over unauthorized loans; certified California fee class action pending; deferred-interest promotions need careful disclosure
providers.reputation_flag: GreenSky has faced federal and state action over loans taken out in consumers' names without their authorization. On July 12, 2021 the CFPB issued a consent order finding GreenSky engaged in origination activity on thousands of loans consumers did not request or authorize; GreenSky paid a $2.5 million civil penalty and was ordered to provide up to $9 million in refunds or loan cancellations. In May 2026 GreenSky settled an investigation by Texas, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Alaska and the District of Columbia into complaints that businesses offering its loans took them out in consumers' names without consent and into GreenSky's oversight of those businesses; Alaska's attorney general says the settlement sets up restitution of up to $6 million in cash or credit to consumers. In Belyea v. GreenSky (N.D. Cal.), a federal judge on January 2, 2025 certified a class of California borrowers on claims over GreenSky's transaction fees under state credit-services and financing laws; the case was still active in September 2026. Make sure every customer personally authorizes their loan and understands any deferred-interest terms.
providers.affiliate_payout_note: No confirmed affiliate program; we currently earn nothing from GreenSky

faqs.q: How much does GreenSky cost contractors?
faqs.a: Merchants pay GreenSky a transaction fee on each financed sale, calculated as a percentage of the loan amount and set by GreenSky, according to federal court records. GreenSky's fee schedule could not be read on its site, so get the rate for each plan in writing before you enroll and price it into your jobs.

faqs.q: Who owns GreenSky?
faqs.a: A consortium led by Sixth Street, with KKR, Bayview Asset Management and CardWorks, bought GreenSky from Goldman Sachs; the deal closed on March 15, 2024. GreenSky is based in Atlanta.

faqs.q: Does GreenSky lend the money directly?
faqs.a: No. GreenSky administers the program and bank partners fund the loans. A 2026 KBRA release names Synovus Bank and Comenity Capital Bank as originators. Loan proceeds go to the contractor, and the customer repays over time.

faqs.q: What regulatory issues has GreenSky had?
faqs.a: In 2021 the CFPB fined GreenSky $2.5 million and ordered up to $9 million in refunds or cancellations over loans consumers did not request or authorize. In May 2026 it settled a multistate investigation (Texas, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Alaska and DC) over loans businesses took out in consumers' names without consent, with up to $6 million in consumer redress according to Alaska's attorney general.

faqs.q: GreenSky vs Wisetack?
faqs.a: Wisetack publishes its merchant fee (3.9% per financed job, more for longer 0% APR add-ons) and covers jobs from $500 to $65,000. GreenSky's transaction fee is set by GreenSky and not published, and its programs include deferred-interest promotional loans. Compare written terms from both before choosing.

providers.name: Hearth
providers.tagline: Contractor software with a multi-lender financing marketplace, sold by annual subscription
providers.pricing_summary: Hearth charges contractors an annual subscription and no per-loan dealer fee. Its pricing page lists Hearth Pro, Pro + Harper and Enterprise with no prices (demo only); Hearth comparison pages updated July 2026 cite $1,499-$4,999 a year on one page and $2,000-$6,000 a year plus a one-time $99 setup fee on another. Homeowners see offers from 18+ lenders: loans of $1,000-$250,000 from 7.99% APR over up to 12 years, plus 0% intro APR credit cards for 6-18 months.
providers.apr_range: From 7.99% APR (personal loans via 18+ lenders); rates set by each lender, plus 0% intro APR credit cards for 6-18 months
providers.contractor_cost: Annual subscription with no per-loan dealer fee. Plan prices are demo-only; Hearth pages updated July 2026 cite $1,499-$4,999/yr on one page and $2,000-$6,000/yr plus a $99 setup fee on another.
providers.long_description:
Hearth is contractor software built around a consumer-financing marketplace. It is the trade name of Shogun Enterprises Inc. in Austin, Texas, and its team page lists Anthony Ghosn and Joe Lonsdale as co-founders. Hearth is licensed as a broker where state law requires (NMLS ID 1628533) and says it does not accept credit applications, make loans or make credit decisions; its lending partners set rates, terms and fees.

Homeowners prequalify through a soft credit pull that Hearth says does not affect their score, then see offers from 18+ lenders: personal loans of $1,000 to $250,000 with rates from 7.99% APR and terms of up to 12 years, or 0% intro APR credit cards for 6-18 months. Hearth says its lenders serve FICO scores down to 550. Loan funds go directly to the customer, and the contractor is paid for the job as usual.

Instead of a per-loan dealer fee, the contractor pays an annual subscription. The pricing page lists three plans with no prices: Hearth Pro (financing, quotes with monthly payments, client management, Hearth Pay and concierge support), Pro + Harper (adds Harper, an AI assistant that answers calls 24/7, follows up with leads and helps with loan follow-up) and Enterprise (adds a dedicated account manager and implementation help). Hearth's own comparison pages, updated July 2026, cite $1,499-$4,999 a year on one page and $2,000-$6,000 a year plus a $99 setup fee on another.

The trade-off: the subscription is a fixed cost whether you finance one job or fifty, and prices are only quoted on a demo call. Hearth pays off for contractors who finance enough work, or use enough of the bundled tools, to cover the annual fee.
providers.how_it_works: You sign up for a Hearth plan after a demo; payment and refund terms are set in Hearth's Contractor Agreement. From Hearth you send a customer a financing link or a quote with monthly payments built in. The customer prequalifies with a soft credit pull that Hearth says does not affect their score and sees offers from 18+ lenders: loans of $1,000-$250,000 from 7.99% APR over up to 12 years, or 0% intro APR credit cards for 6-18 months. The customer applies with the chosen lender, which may run a hard credit check. Hearth says approved funds are typically disbursed within a day directly to the customer, who then pays you for the job. There is no per-loan dealer fee.

pros_detail.title: No per-loan dealer fee
pros_detail.explanation: Hearth says it charges no dealer fees, whatever the customer's credit score. You pay the subscription instead of a percentage of each financed job.

pros_detail.title: Offers from 18+ lenders
pros_detail.explanation: Customers see personal-loan offers of $1,000-$250,000 from 7.99% APR, and Hearth says its lenders serve FICO scores down to 550.

pros_detail.title: 0% intro APR card options
pros_detail.explanation: Qualified homeowners can also see 0% intro APR credit card offers for 6-18 months, per Hearth.

pros_detail.title: Soft-pull prequalification
pros_detail.explanation: Hearth says prequalifying does not affect the customer's credit score; a lender may run a hard check only when the customer applies.

pros_detail.title: Software bundled with financing
pros_detail.explanation: Plans include quotes with monthly payments, client management and Hearth Pay, and the Pro + Harper plan adds an AI assistant that answers calls 24/7 and follows up with leads.

cons_detail.title: Fixed annual cost
cons_detail.explanation: The subscription is owed whether or not customers finance. Hearth's own pages cite $1,499-$4,999 a year on one page and $2,000-$6,000 a year plus a $99 setup fee on another.

cons_detail.title: Prices only on a demo call
cons_detail.explanation: The pricing page lists plans without prices, and payment and refund terms are set in a separate Contractor Agreement, so read that agreement before signing.

cons_detail.title: Broker, not lender
cons_detail.explanation: Hearth does not make loans or credit decisions. Rates, approvals and servicing depend on whichever lender the customer picks.

cons_detail.title: Money goes to the customer
cons_detail.explanation: Loan funds are paid to the homeowner, not to you, so you still collect payment for the job from the customer.

cons_detail.title: BBB complaint volume
cons_detail.explanation: Hearth's BBB profile lists 97 complaints closed in the last three years (checked 30 September 2026). Read recent complaints before committing to an annual plan.

providers.best_for: Contractors who finance enough jobs, or will use enough of the bundled quoting, payments and AI call-answering tools, to justify an annual subscription instead of paying a per-loan dealer fee
providers.weaknesses: Annual subscription is a fixed cost and prices are demo-only; Hearth's own pages quote different price ranges; loan funds go to the customer, not the contractor; 97 BBB complaints closed in three years
providers.reputation_flag: Hearth's BBB profile lists 97 complaints closed in the last three years (checked 30 September 2026). Hearth has been BBB-accredited since October 2017. Its terms of use say payment and refund terms are governed by a separate Hearth Contractor Agreement, and contractors may be eligible for a 60-day money-back guarantee; read the agreement's renewal and cancellation terms before you sign.
providers.affiliate_payout_note: No confirmed affiliate program; we currently earn nothing from Hearth

faqs.q: How does Hearth charge contractors?
faqs.a: Hearth uses an annual subscription and charges no per-loan dealer fee. The pricing page lists Hearth Pro, Pro + Harper and Enterprise without prices. Hearth's comparison pages, updated July 2026, cite $1,499-$4,999 a year on one page and $2,000-$6,000 a year plus a one-time $99 setup fee on another, so ask for a written quote.

faqs.q: Does Hearth make the loans?
faqs.a: No. Hearth says it is a technology company licensed as a broker where state law requires (NMLS ID 1628533). It does not accept credit applications, make loans or make credit decisions. Its 18+ lending partners set the APRs (from 7.99%), terms and fees.

faqs.q: What can my customers borrow through Hearth?
faqs.a: Personal loans of $1,000 to $250,000 with terms of up to 12 years and rates from 7.99% APR, depending on credit, plus 0% intro APR credit cards for 6-18 months. Hearth says prequalifying does not affect the customer's credit score.

faqs.q: Who gets the loan money?
faqs.a: The customer. Hearth says financing is disbursed directly to your customer, typically within a day of approval, and you get paid for the job as usual. The customer repays the lender.

faqs.q: Hearth vs Wisetack?
faqs.a: Wisetack charges a fee on each financed job (3.9%, more for longer 0% APR add-ons) and covers jobs up to $65,000. Hearth charges an annual subscription with no per-loan fee and shows offers of up to $250,000 from 18+ lenders. Low-volume contractors may pay less per job with a per-transaction model; high-volume contractors may come out ahead with a subscription.

providers.name: Acorn Finance
providers.tagline: Free-to-contractor lending marketplace: customers compare offers from 20+ lenders
providers.pricing_summary: Free for contractors: Acorn says it charges no setup, platform, monthly or dealer fees, and its terms say it may be paid lead generation fees by its lending partners. Customers check offers from 20+ lenders with no credit-score impact; loan amounts, APRs and terms are set by each lender.
providers.apr_range: Varies by lender and customer credit; set in each lender's own offer and disclosures
providers.loan_range: Varies by lender; amounts and terms are set in each lender's offer
providers.contractor_cost: Free: Acorn says no setup, platform, monthly or dealer fees
providers.long_description:
Acorn Finance is an online lending marketplace that contractors use to offer customer financing at no cost to the contractor. It is the trade name of Headway Sales Inc., based in Sacramento, California, and its about page says it was founded in 2018 by CEO Giri Addanki. Acorn says it is not a lender and does not make loans or credit decisions; its terms say lending partners may pay it lead generation fees.

A contractor signs up online and shares a financing link, or offers Acorn inside partner software such as JobTread and AccuLynx. The customer checks offers from Acorn's 20+ lending partners, which Acorn says takes under a minute and has no credit-score impact; a hard credit check happens only when the customer proceeds with a lender. Acorn's partner page names personal-loan lenders such as LightStream, SoFi, LendingClub, Upgrade and Prosper, plus line-of-credit, secured-loan and merchant lending partners.

Acorn says partner lenders must deliver funds within 48 hours of approval. The money goes to the customer, and Acorn's contractor FAQ says the customer pays the contractor from the loan proceeds, within 1 to 2 business days after project approval. Loan amounts, APRs and terms come from each lender's own offer, so they vary widely with the lender and the customer's credit.

The trade-off: offering Acorn costs the contractor nothing, but you do not control which lender or rate the customer gets, and you collect payment from the customer rather than from a lender.
providers.how_it_works: You sign up online at no cost and get a financing link to share, or use Acorn inside JobTread or AccuLynx. The customer enters their details and checks offers from 20+ lenders with no credit-score impact; the chosen lender runs a hard credit check when the customer proceeds. Acorn says partner lenders must fund within 48 hours of approval. The funds go to the customer, who pays you from the loan proceeds; Acorn's FAQ says contractors are paid within 1 to 2 business days after project approval. You pay no setup, monthly or dealer fees; Acorn may be paid by the lenders.

pros_detail.title: No cost to the contractor
pros_detail.explanation: Acorn says there are no setup, platform, monthly or dealer fees for contractors. Its revenue comes from lead generation fees paid by lending partners, per its terms.

pros_detail.title: 20+ lenders in one application
pros_detail.explanation: Customers see offers from Acorn's 20+ lending partners, including personal-loan lenders such as LightStream, SoFi, LendingClub, Upgrade and Prosper.

pros_detail.title: No credit impact to check offers
pros_detail.explanation: Acorn says checking offers does not affect the customer's credit score; a hard check happens only with the lender the customer picks.

pros_detail.title: Fast funding requirement
pros_detail.explanation: Acorn says partner lenders must deliver funds within 48 hours of approval, and contractors are typically paid within 1 to 2 business days after project approval.

pros_detail.title: Works inside some contractor software
pros_detail.explanation: Acorn has partner pages for JobTread, where loan offers appear in estimates, and AccuLynx, where offers appear on estimates and invoices.

cons_detail.title: Money goes to the customer
cons_detail.explanation: Loan funds are paid to the homeowner, who then pays you, so you still have to collect for the job.

cons_detail.title: Rates vary widely by lender
cons_detail.explanation: APRs, amounts and terms are set by each lender and depend on the customer's credit. Some partners are line-of-credit providers, so customers should compare the APR on every offer.

cons_detail.title: Lighter software integration
cons_detail.explanation: Acorn names only a few software partners (such as JobTread and AccuLynx); otherwise you share a link rather than offering financing from inside your field-service app.

cons_detail.title: Experience depends on the lender
cons_detail.explanation: Acorn does not make loans or credit decisions, so approval, funding and servicing depend on whichever lender the customer chooses.

providers.best_for: Contractors who want to offer customer financing at no cost, let customers compare offers from many lenders, and are comfortable collecting payment from the customer after the loan funds
providers.weaknesses: Loan funds go to the customer, not the contractor; rates and amounts vary by lender and credit; few named software integrations
providers.affiliate_payout_note: No confirmed affiliate program; we currently earn nothing from Acorn Finance

faqs.q: Is Acorn Finance really free for contractors?
faqs.a: Acorn says it charges contractors no setup, platform, monthly or dealer fees. Its terms say it may be paid lead generation fees by its lending partners, and its site says offers come from third-party advertisers that compensate Acorn.

faqs.q: How does Acorn Finance work for my customers?
faqs.a: The customer uses your link, enters their details and sees offers from Acorn's 20+ lending partners. Acorn says checking offers takes under a minute and does not affect their credit score; the chosen lender does a hard credit check when they proceed. Rates, amounts and terms come from each lender.

faqs.q: When does the contractor get paid?
faqs.a: Acorn says partner lenders must deliver funds within 48 hours of approval. The funds go to the customer, and Acorn's contractor FAQ says the customer pays the contractor from the loan proceeds within 1 to 2 business days after project approval.

faqs.q: Acorn Finance vs Hearth?
faqs.a: Both show customers offers from many lenders with a soft-pull check, and in both the loan money goes to the customer. Acorn is free to contractors. Hearth charges an annual subscription with no per-loan fee, and bundles quoting, payments and an AI call-answering assistant.

faqs.q: Acorn Finance vs GreenSky?
faqs.a: Acorn is a free marketplace of third-party lenders, and it does not make loans or credit decisions. GreenSky is a single bank-funded program where the contractor pays GreenSky a transaction fee on each financed sale, and its programs include deferred-interest promotional loans.

providers.name: Service Finance Company
providers.tagline: Truist-owned point-of-sale installment lender for home-improvement contractors, with 50+ programs
providers.pricing_summary: Service Finance lends directly under its own license and says it offers more than fifty programs, including no-interest, deferred-interest and long-term installment plans. Dealer fees, customer APRs and loan limits are not published; they are discussed after you submit a dealer sign-up form and take a call.
providers.apr_range: Not published; varies by program (no-interest, deferred-interest and long-term installment plans)
providers.loan_range: Not published; fixed-amount, fixed-term installment loans for home-improvement projects
providers.contractor_cost: Not published; dealer terms are discussed on a call after the sign-up form
providers.long_description:
Service Finance Company, LLC is a point-of-sale lender for home-improvement contractors. It describes itself as a nationally licensed sales finance company and an approved FHA Title I lender (NMLS 140908), and its privacy notice says it is a subsidiary of Truist; Truist announced the acquisition in 2021. Its mailing address is in Boca Raton, Florida.

Service Finance says it offers more than fifty financing programs with promotional and standard installment terms, including no-interest, deferred-interest and long-term installment plans. The loans are fixed-amount, fixed-term installment loans, not revolving credit lines. It says it finances over 500 home-improvement products and services, including roofing, insulation, HVAC, kitchen and bath remodeling, windows and doors, flooring, fences, sheds and pools.

Dealers apply through a sign-up form and a follow-up call, then offer financing through a dealer portal or the Service Finance dealer app for iOS and Android. Customers make payments by mail, through an online borrower portal or by phone, using check, ACH, money order or cashier's check; Service Finance does not accept credit or debit card payments.

The trade-off: you get a bank-owned lender with a deep program menu, but dealer fees, customer APRs and loan limits are not published, so you only learn the cost after the sales call.
providers.how_it_works: You submit Service Finance's business sign-up form and a representative calls to discuss enrollment. Once enrolled, you present financing to the homeowner during the sale through the dealer portal or the dealer mobile app. Service Finance lends directly under its own licenses, with programs that include no-interest, deferred-interest and long-term installment plans, each a fixed-amount, fixed-term installment loan. The customer then repays Service Finance by mail, online through its borrower portal, or by phone. Dealer fees and customer rates are set in your dealer agreement and are not published.

providers.name: Foundation Finance Company
providers.tagline: Home-improvement installment financing with first and second looks across credit tiers
providers.pricing_summary: Foundation Finance Company is a direct lender offering closed-end installment contracts for home-improvement projects. Foundation says it is free to join its dealer network, with no monthly charges or volume requirements. Contracts go up to $100,000 over 12-240 months, with options for customers with FICOs as low as 550. Foundation does not publish its APRs or dealer fees; it offers low-fee rate buy-downs, same-as-cash promotions and no-fee options.
providers.apr_range: Not published; fixed-rate installment contracts, rates vary by credit tier, promotion and dealer
providers.contractor_cost: Free to join, no monthly charges or volume requirements. Tier 1 and 2 approvals pay out 100% with no risk discount; Tier 3-5 risk discounts vary by credit and application. Promotional and buy-down fees are not published.
providers.long_description:
Foundation Finance Company is a Wisconsin-based lender that offers point-of-sale financing for home-improvement contractors. It was founded in 2012 through a partnership of a management team and Garrison Investment Group, and in September 2022 InterVest Capital Partners, a New York specialty finance investor, acquired it from Garrison. Foundation says it operates in all 50 states and that its dealer network has more than 8,500 contractors.

The product is a fixed-rate, closed-end installment contract of up to $100,000 with terms of 12-240 months and no prepayment penalty. Foundation says it approves across five credit tiers, with options for customers with FICOs as low as 550, and it offers second look financing that can use the signed application a customer already submitted to another lender. Its markets list covers home improvement, HVAC, remodeling, roofing, siding, solar and energy efficiency, turf, water treatment and windows.

For the contractor, Foundation says joining is free, takes less than five minutes and carries no monthly charges or volume requirements. Tier 1 and 2 approvals pay out 100% with no risk discount, while Tier 3-5 approvals carry a risk discount that varies with the customer's credit and application. Promotions include reduced rates, same-as-cash, deferred payments and no payments-no interest, and Foundation says no-fee options are also available.

The trade-off: Foundation publishes neither its APR range nor its dealer fees or risk discounts, so a contractor only learns the true cost of each tier and promotion after enrolling. Get the fee schedule in writing and explain the customer's rate clearly, since lower-tier approvals are priced for higher credit risk.
providers.how_it_works: The contractor sends the customer a custom credit application link by text or email, or posts it on a website. The customer can prequalify with a soft credit pull; driver's license scanning fills in the application. Contract documents go out through DocuSign, the contractor completes the job, Foundation makes a customer verification call, and the contractor is paid by ACH. Declined applications from another lender can be submitted for a second look.

pros_detail.title: Approvals across credit tiers
pros_detail.explanation: Foundation says it approves across five tiers, with options for customers with FICOs as low as 550, plus second look financing for applicants declined elsewhere.

pros_detail.title: Free to join
pros_detail.explanation: Foundation says enrolling is free, takes less than five minutes and has no monthly charges or volume requirements.

pros_detail.title: Large projects and long terms
pros_detail.explanation: Installment contracts go up to $100,000 with terms of 12-240 months and no prepayment penalty.

pros_detail.title: Paperless workflow
pros_detail.explanation: Soft-pull prequalification, driver's license scanning, DocuSign contracts and the LaunchPAD dealer portal for tracking applications.

pros_detail.title: Range of promotions
pros_detail.explanation: Reduced-rate, same-as-cash, deferred-payment and no payments-no interest plans, including options Foundation describes as no-fee.

cons_detail.title: No published APRs
cons_detail.explanation: Foundation does not publish an APR range, so customer rates are only known per approval.

cons_detail.title: Dealer costs not published
cons_detail.explanation: Risk discounts for Tier 3-5 approvals and promotion fees are not published; confirm them in writing before relying on them.

cons_detail.title: Paid after verification
cons_detail.explanation: Funding comes by ACH only after the job is complete and Foundation's customer verification call.

cons_detail.title: Home-improvement focus
cons_detail.explanation: Its markets list covers home improvement, HVAC, remodeling, roofing, siding, solar, turf, water treatment and windows, not general service or repair work.

providers.weaknesses: No published APR range; Tier 3-5 risk discounts and promotion fees not published; payment only after job completion and a verification call; home-improvement markets only

providers.affiliate_payout_note: Contractor enrolls as a dealer; not an affiliate-link model

faqs.q: Who owns Foundation Finance?
faqs.a: InterVest Capital Partners, a New York specialty finance investor, acquired Foundation Finance from Garrison Investment Group in September 2022, according to Foundation's own press release. Foundation was founded in 2012 and is based in Rothschild, Wisconsin.

faqs.q: How much does Foundation Finance cost a contractor?
faqs.a: Foundation says it is free to join its dealer network, with no monthly charges or volume requirements. Tier 1 and 2 approvals pay out 100% with no risk discount; Tier 3-5 approvals carry a risk discount that varies by credit and application. Foundation does not publish those discounts or its promotion fees, so get your schedule in writing.

faqs.q: What loan sizes and terms does Foundation Finance offer?
faqs.a: Installment contracts for projects up to $100,000, with terms of 12-240 months and no prepayment penalty. Foundation does not publish an APR range; rates, terms and promotions vary by dealer and credit tier.

providers.name: Synchrony HOME
providers.tagline: Synchrony Bank revolving credit for home projects, with deferred-interest and fixed-APR promotions
providers.pricing_summary: Revolving promotional credit issued by Synchrony Bank. For contractors, Synchrony now leads with the Synchrony Project Card (special financing for 6 to 132 months); the Synchrony HOME card is its general home card at retail partners. The merchant fee depends on the promotion: Synchrony's published 2026 York program lists standard fees from 0% to 23.45% by plan. The HOME card's standard purchase APR is 34.99% for new accounts as of 7/31/2025.
providers.apr_range: 0% deferred-interest or reduced fixed-APR promotions; standard HOME card purchase APR 34.99%, penalty APR 39.99% (new accounts as of 7/31/2025)
providers.loan_range: Revolving credit line set at approval; Synchrony does not publish a maximum. Project Card promotions run 6 to 132 months
providers.contractor_cost: Merchant fee per financed sale, set by the promotion. Synchrony's 2026 York program lists 4.45%-10.10% for 6-24 month deferred interest, 0%-22.10% for fixed-APR plans and 10.85%-23.45% for 25-72 month no-interest plans, before manufacturer rebates. Other programs' fees are not published.
providers.long_description:
Synchrony HOME is part of Synchrony's home-improvement financing, a revolving credit program issued by Synchrony Bank, the banking subsidiary of Stamford, Connecticut-based Synchrony Financial (NYSE: SYF). Synchrony says it serves tens of thousands of home improvement businesses. For contractors, Synchrony's home improvement page now leads with the Synchrony Project Card, which offers special financing for 6 to 132 months and is accepted at thousands of contractor locations; the Synchrony HOME card is Synchrony's general home card, accepted at retail partners for furniture, flooring, appliances and more.

Customers apply on the contractor's device, their own device or the contractor's website, and Synchrony's financing has been integrated into ServiceTitan since April 2024. The contractor picks which promotions to offer: deferred-interest plans, fixed reduced-APR plans and equal-payment no-interest plans. Contractors manage the program through Synchrony's Business Center and its Toolbox of training and tools.

The cost is a merchant fee that rises with the richness of the promotion. Synchrony's published 2026 program for York HVAC dealers shows the range: 4.45%-10.10% for 6-24 month deferred interest, up to 22.10% for a 3.99% APR fixed-payment plan, and 23.45% for 72 months with no interest. Qualifying York contractors can get rebates of up to 3% or 6%, which bring some plans to 0%. Other programs' fee schedules are not public.

The trade-off: some promotions, including the 6-24 month plans in York's program, are deferred interest. Synchrony's disclosure says interest is charged from the purchase date if the promotional balance is not paid in full within the promotional period, and the HOME card's standard purchase APR is 34.99% for new accounts as of 7/31/2025. Explain those terms to every customer, and get your own fee schedule in writing, since long no-interest plans can cost the contractor more than 20% of the sale.
providers.how_it_works: The contractor fills out Synchrony's merchant form and Synchrony's team follows up within one business day. Once enrolled, the contractor chooses which promotions to offer, and customers apply on the contractor's device, their own device or the contractor's website, or inside ServiceTitan. Approved customers get a revolving credit line and pick a promotional plan; the contractor pays a merchant fee set by that plan and manages sales in Synchrony's Business Center.

pros_detail.title: Wide promotional menu
pros_detail.explanation: Deferred-interest, fixed reduced-APR and equal-payment no-interest plans, with Project Card promotions from 6 to 132 months.

pros_detail.title: Manufacturer rebates
pros_detail.explanation: Some manufacturer programs cut the fee: York's 2026 program gives qualifying contractors rebates of up to 3% or 6%, bringing some plans to 0%.

pros_detail.title: ServiceTitan integration
pros_detail.explanation: Since April 2024, contractors can offer Synchrony financing inside ServiceTitan with direct-to-device applications and pre-fill.

pros_detail.title: Large bank issuer
pros_detail.explanation: Credit is extended by Synchrony Bank, part of publicly traded Synchrony Financial, which reports more than 70 million active customer accounts.

pros_detail.title: Reusable credit line
pros_detail.explanation: Customers get a revolving line they can use again, and the HOME card is accepted at thousands of retail partners.

cons_detail.title: Rich promotions cost more
cons_detail.explanation: In Synchrony's published York program, standard fees reach 10.10% for 24-month deferred interest and 23.45% for 72 months no interest.

cons_detail.title: Deferred-interest risk for customers

cons_detail.title: High standard APR

cons_detail.title: Fee schedules not public

cons_detail.title: Card, not an installment loan

providers.best_for: HVAC, flooring, windows and remodeling contractors, especially dealers in a manufacturer program that rebates Synchrony merchant fees
providers.weaknesses: Merchant fees up to 23.45% on long no-interest plans in the published York program; deferred-interest back-charges if customers miss the promo window; 34.99% standard HOME card APR; fee schedules and credit limits not public; revolving card, not an installment loan
providers.affiliate_program: N/A: "become a Synchrony merchant/partner" (apply online or by phone)
providers.affiliate_payout_note: Contractor enrolls as a merchant; not an affiliate-link model

faqs.q: Is Synchrony HOME a loan or a credit card?
faqs.a: It is revolving credit issued by Synchrony Bank, not a fixed-term installment loan. For contractors, Synchrony now leads with the Synchrony Project Card, with special financing for 6 to 132 months, while the Synchrony HOME card is its general home card at retail partners. Either way the customer gets a reusable credit line with promotional plans.

faqs.q: How much does Synchrony financing cost a contractor?
faqs.a: A merchant fee per financed sale that depends on the promotion. Synchrony's published 2026 York program lists 4.45%-10.10% for 6-24 month deferred-interest plans and up to 23.45% for 72 months no interest, before rebates of up to 3% or 6% for qualifying York dealers. Other programs' fees are not public, so get yours in writing.

The HOME card's standard purchase APR is 34.99% for new accounts as of 7/31/2025, so set clear expectations about paying off before the window closes.

providers.name: Sunbit
providers.tagline: Pay-over-time plans for in-person service businesses, lent by TAB Bank
providers.pricing_summary: Point-of-sale installment plans for in-person service businesses, including home services. Loans are made by TAB Bank: $50-$20,000 over 3-72 months at 0%-35.99% APR, with lower caps in some states. Sunbit does not publish its direct merchant fee; through Stripe, Sunbit is priced at 6% + 30 cents per successful charge. The business is paid up front.
providers.apr_range: 0%-35.99% APR; lower caps in some states, and 0% plans are not available at all merchants
providers.loan_range: $50-$20,000; terms 3-72 months (largest amounts and longest terms not available at all merchants)
providers.contractor_cost: Direct merchant fee not published by Sunbit. Through Stripe: 6% + 30 cents per successful Sunbit charge.
providers.long_description:
Sunbit offers pay-over-time plans at the point of sale for in-person service businesses. Sunbit says it was founded in 2016 and is available at more than 30,000 locations; its home services line sits alongside automotive, dental, eyewear, veterinary and other verticals. The loans are made by Transportation Alliance Bank (TAB Bank); Sunbit's disclosures state that Sunbit Now, LLC is not the lender.

Sunbit's disclosures cover loans of $50-$20,000 over 3-72 months at 0%-35.99% APR, with lower caps in several states. A payment is due at checkout, and Sunbit says it charges customers no application, origination, prepayment or late fees. Checking eligibility is a soft credit inquiry, and Sunbit says 90% of people are approved. 0% plans, the largest amounts and the longest terms are not available at every merchant; its how-it-works page shows 3, 6 or 12-month plans, with longer terms for dental care.

Contractors can offer Sunbit directly or through software. In 2026 Sunbit became generally available nationwide in the Stripe Dashboard for in-person service businesses, where customers choose 3, 6, 12 or 18-month plans on transactions from $60 to $19,999.99, and Workiz lists Sunbit as one of its consumer financing providers. Sunbit says it takes the repayment and fraud risk, and the business is paid up front.

The trade-off: Sunbit does not publish its direct merchant fee, and the one published price, 6% + 30 cents per charge through Stripe, is higher than some flat-fee alternatives. The $20,000 ceiling rules it out for large remodels and roofs, and customer APRs can reach 35.99%, so it fits repair and service tickets better than big projects.
providers.how_it_works: At checkout the customer applies with a soft credit inquiry, picks a monthly plan and makes a payment due at checkout. TAB Bank makes the loan, the business is paid up front, and Sunbit collects the monthly payments. Through Stripe, the customer is redirected to Sunbit to choose a 3, 6, 12 or 18-month plan; Sunbit says funds are sent immediately and can take 2-5 business days to reach the bank account.

pros_detail.title: Soft credit check
pros_detail.explanation: Checking eligibility is a soft inquiry that does not affect the customer's credit score, and Sunbit says 90% of people are approved.

pros_detail.title: Paid up front
pros_detail.explanation: The business is paid up front; Sunbit says it takes the repayment and fraud risk.

pros_detail.title: Covers small tickets
pros_detail.explanation: Loans start at $50 ($60 through Stripe), which suits repair and service calls.

pros_detail.title: No customer penalty fees
pros_detail.explanation: Sunbit says customers pay no application, origination, prepayment or late fees.

pros_detail.title: Available in Stripe and Workiz
pros_detail.explanation: Sunbit is generally available in the Stripe Dashboard, and Workiz lists it as a consumer financing provider.

cons_detail.title: Merchant fee not published
cons_detail.explanation: Sunbit does not publish its direct merchant fee; through Stripe it costs 6% + 30 cents per successful charge.

cons_detail.title: $20,000 ceiling
cons_detail.explanation: Loans top out at $20,000, and the largest amounts are not available at every merchant, so it does not fit large remodels or roofs.

cons_detail.title: APRs up to 35.99%
cons_detail.explanation: Customers who do not get a 0% plan can pay up to 35.99% APR, less in some states.

cons_detail.title: Short plans outside dental care
cons_detail.explanation: Terms reach 72 months in the disclosures, but Sunbit shows 3, 6 or 12-month plans outside dental care, and Stripe offers 3-18 months.

cons_detail.title: Not home-improvement specific
cons_detail.explanation: Home services is one of many Sunbit verticals, alongside automotive, dental and eyewear.

providers.best_for: Repair and service work (HVAC service calls, plumbing, electrical, pool and appliance repair) with tickets under $20,000, especially businesses already taking payments through Stripe
providers.weaknesses: Direct merchant fee not published (6% + 30 cents via Stripe); $20,000 ceiling; APRs up to 35.99%; short plan terms outside dental care; home services is one of many verticals
providers.affiliate_program: N/A: merchant/partner signup, often via an integrated field-service or payment platform
providers.affiliate_payout_note: Contractor enrolls as a merchant; not an affiliate-link model

faqs.q: What kind of jobs is Sunbit best for?
faqs.a: Smaller in-person service jobs such as HVAC service calls, plumbing, electrical and appliance repair. Sunbit's disclosures cover loans of $50-$20,000, so it does not fit large remodels or roofs.

faqs.q: How much does Sunbit cost a contractor?
faqs.a: Sunbit does not publish its direct merchant fee, so ask for it in writing. If you take Sunbit through Stripe, Stripe prices it at 6% + 30 cents per successful charge. Either way the business is paid up front.

faqs.q: Does applying for Sunbit hurt my customer's credit?
faqs.a: No. Sunbit says checking eligibility is a soft credit inquiry that does not affect the customer's credit score. Loans are made by TAB Bank at 0%-35.99% APR, with lower caps in some states, and 0% plans are not available at all merchants.

providers.name: Regions | EnerBank Home Improvement Financing
providers.tagline: Regions Bank home-improvement loans for established remodelers, non-recourse to the contractor
providers.pricing_summary: Bank lender: Regions Home Improvement Financing (formerly EnerBank USA) is part of Regions Bank. Regions says there are no fixed or required costs, no sign-up fees and no merchant processing fees, but many of its loan products carry a dealer fee; no dealer fee schedule is published. Products: Same-As-Cash, Reduced Interest, Zero Interest and Traditional Installment loans. Regions publishes no APRs or loan amounts.
providers.apr_range: Not published; Zero Interest Loans carry a 0% fixed APR for the full term, other rates set per loan
providers.loan_range: Not published; contractors need an average project size of at least $5,000 to enroll
providers.contractor_cost: No sign-up fees, no fixed or required costs and no merchant processing fees, per Regions. Many loan products carry a dealer fee; Regions does not publish the schedule.
providers.long_description:
Regions Home Improvement Financing is the former EnerBank USA, a Salt Lake City home-improvement lender established in 2002. Regions Bank, based in Birmingham, Alabama, completed its acquisition of EnerBank from CMS Energy on October 1, 2021, and the EnerBank name has since been folded into the Regions brand. At the time EnerBank worked with more than 10,000 contractors in all 50 states, and Regions now says it has funded over $15 billion in home improvement projects.

The contractor offers financing in the customer's home, and Regions Bank makes the loan. Regions says its loans are all non-recourse for the contractor, meaning the bank takes the credit risk, and that funds are usually deposited within 24 hours. Products include Same-As-Cash loans (no interest and no monthly payment during the same-as-cash period, with interest waived if paid in full in time), Reduced Interest loans, Zero Interest loans with equal payments at a 0% fixed APR for the full term, and Traditional Installment loans. Customers can use PreQualify, and apply online, in the mobile app or by phone.

The program is limited to established remodelers. Regions requires a residential remodeling focus, at least five years in business (three with an existing Regions banking relationship), annual residential remodeling sales of at least $500,000 ($300,000 with a Regions relationship), an average project size of at least $5,000, and satisfactory credit and BBB reports. Regions says onboarding can take as little as three weeks, with a dedicated relationship manager.

The trade-off: Regions publishes no APRs, loan amounts or dealer fees. It says there are no sign-up or merchant processing fees, but many of its loan products carry a dealer fee, so get the fee for each product in writing before quoting promotions to customers.
providers.how_it_works: The contractor applies to join a loan program and is onboarded with a dedicated relationship manager, in as little as three weeks according to Regions. The homeowner can use PreQualify, then applies online, in the mobile app or by phone and signs digitally. Regions Bank makes the loan and deposits funds by ACH, usually within 24 hours, and the loans are non-recourse to the contractor.

pros_detail.title: Non-recourse to the contractor
pros_detail.explanation: Regions says its home improvement loans are all non-recourse for the contractor, so the bank takes the credit risk.

pros_detail.title: Bank lender
pros_detail.explanation: Loans come from Regions Bank, which has owned the former EnerBank USA since October 2021.

pros_detail.title: Fast funding
pros_detail.explanation: Regions says funds are usually deposited within 24 hours.

pros_detail.title: Promotional products
pros_detail.explanation: Same-As-Cash, Reduced Interest and Zero Interest loans (0% fixed APR with equal payments) alongside traditional installment loans.

pros_detail.title: Digital tools and support
pros_detail.explanation: PreQualify, a mobile app, digital signatures, the PartnerPortal and a dedicated relationship manager.

cons_detail.title: High bar to enroll
cons_detail.explanation: Five years in business and $500,000 in annual residential remodeling sales (three years and $300,000 with a Regions banking relationship).

cons_detail.title: Larger projects only
cons_detail.explanation: Contractors need an average project size of at least $5,000, so it does not fit small repair tickets.

cons_detail.title: Dealer fees not published
cons_detail.explanation: Many products carry a dealer fee, but Regions does not publish the schedule.

cons_detail.title: No published rates or amounts
cons_detail.explanation: Regions publishes no APR range or loan limits for customers.

cons_detail.title: Onboarding takes time
cons_detail.explanation: Regions says contractors can be offering financing in as little as three weeks, not same day.

providers.best_for: Established residential remodelers (HVAC, roofing, windows, kitchen and bath, foundation repair, hardscaping, fencing) with average projects of $5,000 or more
providers.weaknesses: Requires 5+ years and $500k+ in residential remodeling sales (3 years/$300k with a Regions relationship); $5,000 minimum average project size; dealer fees, APRs and loan amounts not published
providers.affiliate_payout_note: Contractor enrolls as an approved partner; not an affiliate-link model

faqs.q: What does non-recourse mean with Regions home improvement financing?
faqs.a: Regions says its home improvement loans are all non-recourse for the contractor, meaning the bank assumes the credit risk if the homeowner later fails to pay. Funds are usually deposited within 24 hours.

faqs.q: Can any contractor sign up for Regions home improvement financing?
faqs.a: No. Regions requires a residential remodeling focus, at least five years in business and $500,000 in annual residential remodeling sales (three years and $300,000 with an existing Regions banking relationship), an average project size of at least $5,000, and satisfactory credit and BBB reports.

faqs.q: What does Regions home improvement financing cost a contractor?
faqs.a: Regions says there are no sign-up fees, no fixed or required costs and no merchant processing fees. Many of its loan products carry a dealer fee, which Regions says is clearly communicated but does not publish, so confirm each product's fee in your program agreement.

providers.name: PowerPay
providers.tagline: Point-of-sale financing platform for home improvement and patient care, funded by partner lenders
providers.pricing_summary: PowerPay is a point-of-sale financing platform: loans are originated by its lending partners and serviced by PowerPay. PowerPay's readable pages publish no APRs, loan limits, terms or contractor fees; confirm them when you enroll. For borrowers, PowerPay advertises fixed monthly payments with no prepayment penalties, and its account opening disclosures list a one-time $99 account activation fee where applicable.
providers.apr_range: Not published; rates set per loan by PowerPay's lending partners
providers.loan_range: Not published on PowerPay's readable pages; confirm limits and terms when you enroll
providers.contractor_cost: Not published; confirm contractor fees in your PowerPay provider agreement
providers.long_description:
PowerPay is a point-of-sale financing platform based in Wayne, Pennsylvania, founded by Mike Petrakis. It finances home improvement projects such as kitchens, roofs, windows, HVAC and pools, and also offers patient financing for dental, fertility, vision and other elective care. PowerPay says loans are originated by its lending partners and serviced by PowerPay, and in October 2025 it said it provides financing for 15,000 contractors and physician networks.

For the homeowner, PowerPay advertises near-instant credit decisions, electronic loan documents, low fixed monthly payments and no prepayment penalties, with the first payment due about 30 days after funding. The provider is paid directly. PowerPay's account opening disclosures also list a one-time $99 account activation fee where applicable.

PowerPay funds its growth through the capital markets: it completed a $118.9 million securitization in 2024, announced one targeted in the $500 million range in October 2025, and KBRA assigned preliminary ratings to PowerPay Issuance Trust 2026-1 in September 2026.

The trade-off: PowerPay's readable pages do not publish APRs, loan limits, terms or contractor fees, so you only see the real cost and the maximum loan after enrolling. Get the fee schedule and the loan limits in writing, and check whether the $99 activation fee applies to your customers.
providers.how_it_works: The contractor enrolls as a PowerPay provider and offers financing at the point of sale. The customer applies online for a near-instant credit decision and, if approved, signs the loan documents electronically. The loan is originated by one of PowerPay's lending partners, the provider is paid directly, and PowerPay services the loan, with the first payment due about 30 days after funding.

faqs.q: How does PowerPay work?
faqs.a: PowerPay is a point-of-sale financing platform. PowerPay says applications on its platform are originated by one of its lending partners and serviced by PowerPay. The customer gets a near-instant decision, signs electronically, and the provider is paid directly.

faqs.q: What does PowerPay cost a contractor?
faqs.a: PowerPay's readable pages do not publish contractor fees, APRs or loan limits, so confirm them in your provider agreement before offering it. On the customer side, PowerPay advertises no prepayment penalties, and its disclosures list a one-time $99 account activation fee where applicable.

faqs.q: Who is behind PowerPay?
faqs.a: PowerPay was founded by Mike Petrakis and is based in Wayne, Pennsylvania. It finances home improvement and patient care, and in October 2025 said it serves 15,000 contractors and physician networks.
